The two major starches are amylose, consisting of linear segments with a-1,4 glycosidic bonds, and amylopectin, which is
a complex form of starch, consisting of both linear and branched segments with a-1,6 glycosidic bonds (Gray, 2000). The active
enzyme amylase binds to the interior glycosidic bonds of amylose and speciﬁcally to ﬁve consecutive glucose subunits with high
afﬁnity, leading to the production of pentasaccharides (oligosaccharides with ﬁve glucose units linked together) (Leturque and
Brot-Laroche, 2013). The resulting pentasaccharide is hydrolyzed to produce the trisaccharide maltotriose and the disaccharide
maltose, which are the ﬁnal products of amylose digestion and cannot be broken down by the amylase due to low afﬁnity for
the enzyme’s active site (Gray, 2000).
Amylopectin is also digested by amylase, but results in different end products than those of amylose. While amylase binds and
cleaves the a-1,4 glycosidic bonds of amylose, it cannot bind and cleave the a-1,6 glycosidic bonds of amylopectin nor can it bind to
